question: The Alboran Sea is a particularly important area for Mediterranean fisheries and a key corridor for highly migratory species between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Moroccan vessels’ continued use of driftnets – despite a ban under the applicable legislation – has been documented. The risk of by-catch when fishing with driftnets is high. What is more, products caught using banned gear could end up on the EU market. In view of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of Moroccan vessels’ use of driftnets in the Alboran Sea, particularly the cases documented in waters under Spanish jurisdiction?
Is the Commission assessing, within the framework of the IUU Regulation, the extent of Morocco’s compliance and cooperation and is there cause to initiate a yellow-card procedure?

With a view to preventing products obtained by illegal fishing from entering the European market, is the Commission considering, in cooperation with Spain and through the European Fisheries Control Agency, bolstering fisheries control, inspection and surveillance in the Alboran Sea, and stepping up controls on imports from those fisheries?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.11.2026) The Commission is aware of these cases through agreed notifications and inspection reports issued under the Mediterranean Joint Deployment Plan (JDP) and the International Joint Inspection Scheme agreed within the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas.

Within the framework of the Mediterranean JDP risk assessment exercise carried out by the European Fisheries Control Agency (EFCA) and Member States, the non-European fleet operating with driftnets in the Mediterranean has been identified as high risk for non-compliance with gear requirements and the use of illegal gears.

As a result, control, deployment and inspection activities under the JDP target this fleet as a priority. In 2026, following the deployment of the EFCA patrol vessel together with inspectors from Member State authorities, two Moroccan fishing vessels using driftnets1 on the Mediterranean high seas were inspected and reported to the Moroccan authorities.

The Commission regularly assesses the information received on alleged illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing activities. Any pre-identification of non-cooperating third countries must be based on substantial evidence of persistent and systematic failure to prevent and address IUU fishing activities and non-cooperation.

Member States are primarily responsible for the controls of fishery products entering the EU market in accordance with the EU IUU Regulation2. It is up to Member State competent authorities to take the necessary actions if any doubts or concerns are raised as regards the legality of the fishery products imported into their country.
The Commission provides tools to help Member States with risk assessment, including through the digital system CATCH.
1 Under the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) Joint International Scheme,

these vessels were spotted using driftnets with no authorisation and having caught Swordfish in contravention of ICCAT and GFCM (General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean) provisions. The inspection reports were submitted to the Moroccan authorities for follow-up actions. 2 See Chapter III of the Council Regulation (EC) No 1005/2008 of 29 September 2008 establishing a Union system to prevent, deter and eliminate illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing.
